title: The planetary nebula Abell 33 captured using ESO's Very Large Telescope
caption: The planetary nebula Abell 33, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: Abell 33 · constellation Hydra · about 2500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #100 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A blue bubble, almost perfectly round on the sky, lines up with a bright star. The pairing looks uncannily like a diamond engagement ring. This is the planetary nebula Abell 33, captured by astronomers using ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The bubble formed when an ageing star blew off its outer layers. After a Sun-like star runs low on fuel, it sheds its outer gas into space, and the hot core left behind makes that gas glow. The name planetary nebula is a historical accident from early telescopes and has nothing to do with planets.

Two things make Abell 33 special. First, the diamond is a coincidence, because the bright star is in the foreground and just happens to fall in line with the bubble from our point of view. Second, the nebula is unusually symmetric, appearing almost perfectly circular on the sky.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (7.22 x 7.25 arcminutes) and distance (2500 light years), the frame spans roughly 5.3 × 5.3 light-years. Its light set out about 2,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a large telescope collect far more light than the eye, so this faint bubble appears much brighter and more colorful than it would by eye.
